Extremely well-draining soil required (cactus mix with extra perlite). Temperatures above 10°C; bring indoors in cold climates. Feed monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Prune after flowering to shape. Highly toxic to pets and humans — all parts contain cardiac glycosides.

description: Also known as: Tree houseleek. Succulents in the Crassulaceae family with rosette-forming leaves, some varieties are monocarpic.
commonExamples: Aeonium arboreum (Tree houseleek), A. 'Zwartkop' (Black rose), A. haworthii (Pinwheel aeonium), A. 'Kiwi'
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). More water-tolerant than some succulents but still drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with succulent fertilizer. Well-draining soil essential. Some varieties are monocarpic (die after flowering). Repot every 2-3 years. Rosette-forming succulents. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Rosette-forming succulent with thick, fleshy leaves often tipped with spines. Extremely drought tolerant. Many species are monocarpic — they bloom once after many years and then die, but produce offsets (pups).
commonExamples: Agave americana (Century plant), A. attenuata (Fox tail agave), A. victoriae-reginae (Queen Victoria agave), A. parryi (Artichoke agave)
careTips: Water deeply but infrequently — every 2-4 weeks depending on season. Full sun to bright direct light. Very low humidity tolerance. Excellent drainage is critical — use cactus/succulent mix. Cold hardiness varies by species. Mildly toxic — sap can cause skin irritation. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Medicinal aloe. Medicinal succulent with gel-filled leaves, commonly used for skin care.
commonExamples: Aloe vera (Aloe, Medicinal aloe)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Water deeply but infrequently. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with balanced fertilizer at quarter strength. Remove offsets (pups) when 1/3 size of parent to propagate. Repot every 2-3 years. Gel from leaves has medicinal properties for skin care. Overwatering causes rot. Toxic to pets if ingested. Mildly toxic to humans if ingested; gel is safe for topical skin use. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Rosette-forming succulents in the Asphodelaceae family with medicinal properties, many produce offsets (pups) for propagation.
commonExamples: Aloe vera (Medicinal aloe, Burn plant), A. arborescens (Torch aloe, Candelabra aloe), A. polyphylla (Spiral aloe), A. aristata (Lace aloe)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-4 weeks). Water deeply but infrequently. Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with balanced fertilizer at quarter strength. Remove offsets (pups) when they're 1/3 the size of parent plant to propagate. Repot every 2-3 years. Many species have medicinal properties. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Fuzzy succulent with thick, toothed leaves resembling bear paws, tips turn red in bright light. Native to South Africa.
commonExamples: Cotyledon tomentosa (Bear's paw), C. tomentosa subsp. ladismithiensis (Narrow bear's paw)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Very sensitive to overwatering - root rot is the main threat. Bright indirect light preferred; tips turn red with more light exposure. Avoid harsh direct midday sun. Low humidity preferred. Fertilize 2-3 times per year with succulent fertilizer at quarter strength. Excellent drainage essential - use cactus/succulent mix. Handle gently - fuzzy leaves are delicate. Repot every 2-3 years. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Donkey's Tail, Lamb's tail. Trailing succulent with delicate, plump blue-green leaves that drop easily if disturbed.
commonExamples: Sedum morganianum (Burro's tail, Donkey's tail, Lamb's tail)
careTips: Water when soil is dry, but more frequently than most succulents. Handle very carefully - leaves drop easily if disturbed. Water at base to avoid wetting leaves. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun may burn. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot carefully every 2-3 years. Very delicate - avoid moving once established. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Compact jade, Mini jade. Compact jade plant cultivar with smaller leaves; same care as standard jade, ideal for small spaces.
commonExamples: Crassula ovata 'Minor' (Compact jade, Mini jade)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Bright indirect to direct light. Low humidity fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Succulents in the Crassulaceae family with thick fleshy leaves, many form tree-like structures over time.
commonExamples: Crassula ovata (Jade plant, Money tree), C. perforata (String of buttons), C. tetragona (Miniature pine tree), C. arborescens (Silver jade plant)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Water deeply but infrequently. Reduce watering significantly in winter when growth slows. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with balanced fertilizer at quarter strength. Can be trained as bonsai. Repot every 2-3 years. Many form tree-like structures over time. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Rosette-forming succulents with colorful, often powdery leaves, popular in arrangements.
commonExamples: Echeveria elegans, E. 'Perle von Nurnberg', E. agavoides, E. pulidonis
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 1-2 weeks). Water at base to avoid wetting leaves - water on leaves can cause rot. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Remove dead lower leaves. Repot every 2-3 years. Popular in succulent arrangements. Powdery coating (farina) protects from sun - don't rub off. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Striking succulent with thin, pencil-like branches that turn vibrant red-orange in bright light, though actually a euphorbia, not a true cactus.
commonExamples: Euphorbia tirucalli (Pencil cactus, Firestick plant, Milk bush), E. tirucalli 'Sticks on Fire'
careTips: Water sparingly; allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Strong direct light for best color—full sun produces vibrant red tips. Low humidity preferred. Well-draining sandy or gritty succulent mix. Fertilize lightly once in spring. Handle with extreme care—white milky sap is highly irritating to skin and eyes; wear gloves when pruning. Can grow quite large indoors (up to 2 meters). Toxic to pets and humans (caustic latex sap).

description: Also known as: Cathedral cactus. Candelabra-shaped succulent with green stems and leaves; milky sap is toxic—handle with care.
commonExamples: Euphorbia trigona (African milk tree, Cathedral cactus)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Bright indirect light. Low humidity fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year. Toxic sap—wear gloves, wash hands. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Diverse genus including many succulent species with milky sap (toxic, handle with care).
commonExamples: Euphorbia trigona (African milk tree), E. milii (Crown of thorns), E. obesa (Baseball plant)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-4 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with balanced fertilizer at quarter strength. Milky sap is toxic and can cause skin irritation - handle with care and wash hands after touching. Repot every 2-3 years. Diverse genus with many forms. Research specific species for exact requirements. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Tongue-shaped succulents closely related to Haworthia and Aloe in the family Asphodelaceae; shade-tolerant and easy-care.
commonExamples: Gasteria bicolor, G. verrucosa, G. 'Little Warty'
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). More frequent than desert succulents. Bright indirect to medium light preferred; tolerates lower light than most succulents. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 2-3 years. Shade-tolerant and easy-care. Related to Haworthia. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Mother-of-pearl plant. Succulents in the Crassulaceae family with rosette-forming leaves, often called ghost plants.
commonExamples: Graptopetalum paraguayense (Ghost plant, Mother-of-pearl plant), G. 'Copper Rose', G. 'Purple Delight'
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred - more light enhances coloration. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with succulent fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Repot every 2-3 years. Rosette-forming with beautiful coloration. Often called ghost plants. Remove withered and dead leaves and excessive daughter plants

description: Intergeneric hybrid between Graptopetalum and Echeveria, forming compact rosettes with thick, fleshy leaves in pastel hues that intensify with sun stress.
commonExamples: x Graptoveria 'Fred Ives' (Fred Ives), x Graptoveria 'Opalina' (Opalina), x Graptoveria 'Debbie' (Debbie), x Graptoveria 'Bashful' (Bashful)
careTips: Water thoroughly using the soak-and-dry method; allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Provide bright indirect to direct morning light for best coloration — insufficient light causes etiolation. Use a fast-draining cactus or succulent mix with added perlite. Fertilize once in spring and once in mid-summer with a diluted succulent fertilizer. Protect from frost below 5°C. Non-toxic to pets. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

description: Small rosette succulents that tolerate lower light than most succulents, perfect for windowsills.
commonExamples: Haworthia cooperi, H. fasciata (Zebra plant), H. attenuata, H. limifolia
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). More frequent than desert succulents. Bright indirect to medium light preferred; tolerates lower light than most succulents. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 2-3 years. Perfect for windowsills. Small rosette-forming succulents. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Money plant, Lucky plant. Classic succulent with thick, glossy green leaves, can live for decades and grow into a small tree.
commonExamples: Crassula ovata (Jade plant, Money plant, Lucky plant)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Water deeply but infrequently. Bright indirect to direct light preferred - needs good light to maintain compact growth. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with balanced fertilizer at quarter strength. Can live for decades and grow into small tree. Prune to maintain shape. Repot every 2-3 years. Symbol of good luck. Overwatering causes root rot. Toxic to pets.

description: Also known as: Flapjack. Succulent with flat, paddle-shaped leaves that blush red at edges in bright light; monocarpic (dies after flowering).
commonExamples: Kalanchoe luciae (Flapjack, Paddle plant)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Bright light enhances red edges. Low humidity fine. Fertilize sparingly. Toxic to pets. Remove diseased, yellowing and dropping leaves, pinching 1-2 times, germinate more branched

description: Stone-like succulents that mimic pebbles in their native habitat, have specific dormancy periods when they should not be watered.
commonExamples: Lithops (Living stones, Pebble plants), various species with different colors and patterns
careTips: Water sparingly in fall when new leaves emerge. Keep dry in summer dormancy and during winter/spring splitting. Very minimal watering even when active (every 2-4 weeks). Bright direct light essential. Low humidity preferred. Fertilize very sparingly during active growth only. Repot every 3-5 years in very well-draining soil. Stone-like appearance mimics pebbles. Very specific care requirements. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Also known as: Moonstones. Adorable succulents with plump, egg-shaped leaves in pastel shades of lavender, pink, and blue-grey, often covered in a powdery farina coating.
commonExamples: Pachyphytum oviferum (Moonstones, Sugar almond plant), P. compactum (Little jewel), P. bracteosum (Silverbracts)
careTips: Water only when soil is completely dry; soak and drain method works best. Bright indirect to gentle direct light—too much harsh sun can sunburn delicate leaves. Low humidity preferred—prone to rot in damp conditions. Gritty, fast-draining succulent mix essential. Fertilize once in spring with diluted cactus fertilizer. Avoid touching leaves—the farina coating doesn't grow back. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Spekboom. Small-leaved succulent often confused with jade; drought-tolerant, can be bonsai-trained. Native to South Africa.
commonExamples: Portulacaria afra (Dwarf jade, Spekboom, Elephant bush)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Bright indirect to direct light. Low humidity fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Large genus of succulents in the Crassulaceae family, includes both trailing and upright varieties.
commonExamples: Sedum morganianum (Burro's tail), S. rubrotinctum (Jelly bean plant), S. adolphii (Golden sedum), S. 'Autumn Joy'
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with succulent fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Repot every 2-3 years. Many varieties available - trailing and upright. Very easy-care succulents. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Hen and chicks. Hardy succulents in the Crassulaceae family known as hen and chicks, form rosettes and produce offsets. Extremely cold hardy and drought tolerant. Excellent for rock gardens, alpine gardens, and containers.
commonExamples: Sempervivum tectorum (Common houseleek, Hen and chicks), S. arachnoideum (Cobweb houseleek), many cultivars in various colors
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize sparingly (2-3 times per year) with succulent fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Produces offsets (chicks) around parent plant (hen). Repot every 2-3 years. Very cold-hardy succulents. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Large genus of succulents in the Asteraceae family, includes trailing varieties like string of pearls (many reclassified to Curio).
commonExamples: Curio rowleyanus (syn. Senecio rowleyanus; String of pearls), Curio radicans (syn. S. radicans; String of bananas), Curio repens (syn. Senecio serpens; Blue chalk sticks), Curio talinoides subsp. mandraliscae (syn. Senecio mandraliscae)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with succulent fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Many are trailing plants. Repot every 2-3 years. Large genus with many varieties. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Stone-mimicking succulent that resembles a split boulder, closely related to lithops but slightly larger. Native to South Africa.
commonExamples: Pleiospilos nelii (Split rock, Cleft stone, Mimicry plant), P. nelii 'Royal Flush' (purple form)
careTips: Water ONLY when old leaves have fully dried and absorbed into the new pair - typically only 2-4 times per year. Overwatering causes stacking (extra leaf pairs) and rot. Bright direct light essential - at least 5 hours daily. Very low humidity preferred. Do not fertilize. Excellent drainage essential - use mostly mineral substrate (pumice, perlite). Bottom watering preferred. Repot every 3-5 years. Very specific watering requirements similar to lithops. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

description: Trailing succulent with banana-shaped leaves, faster growing than String of Pearls.
commonExamples: Curio radicans (String of bananas, syn. Senecio radicans)
careTips: Water when leaves show slight wrinkling - this indicates thirst. Avoid overwatering which causes rot. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Faster growing than String of Pearls. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Handle carefully to avoid leaf drop. Banana-shaped leaves. Toxic to pets. After flowering remove the withered flowers, the part on the ground will wither in winter, the plant germinates again in spring Trim trailing stems to desired length. Remove any shriveled or dry sections.

description: Also known as: Dolphin Plant, Dolphin Succulent. Trailing succulent with leaves shaped like leaping dolphins.
commonExamples: Curio × peregrinus (String of dolphins, syn. Senecio × peregrinus)
careTips: Water when leaves show slight wrinkling - this indicates thirst. Avoid overwatering which causes rot. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Unique dolphin-shaped leaves. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Handle carefully. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Trailing succulent with heart-shaped leaves and purple undersides, produces tubers along stems.
commonExamples: Ceropegia woodii (String of hearts, Rosary vine, Chain of hearts)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). More drought tolerant than String of Pearls due to tubers along stems. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Produces tubers along stems for storage. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Heart-shaped leaves with purple undersides. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Delicate trailing succulent with thin, needle-like leaves along wiry stems. Related to string of hearts but with a finer, more airy appearance.
commonExamples: Ceropegia linearis (String of needles)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry. Bright indirect light preferred; tolerates some direct morning sun. Low humidity is fine. Very susceptible to overwatering — use well-draining succulent mix. Fertilize lightly spring through summer. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Trailing succulent with bead-like leaves, perfect for hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Curio rowleyanus (String of pearls, syn. Senecio rowleyanus), C. herreianus (String of beads)
careTips: Water when pearls (leaves) show slight wrinkling - this indicates thirst. Avoid overwatering which causes rot. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Bead-like leaves are delicate - handle carefully. Very popular trailing succulent. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Trailing succulent with bean-shaped leaves that turn deep ruby-red in bright light; stems are purple-tinged.
commonExamples: Othonna capensis (String of rubies, Ruby necklace, Little pickles)
careTips: Water thoroughly when soil is completely dry; drought-tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light brings out intense red coloring—green in low light. Low humidity fine. Use well-draining succulent/cactus mix. Fertilize sparingly 2-3 times during growing season at quarter strength. Propagates easily from stem cuttings. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Also known as: Turtle vine. Trailing peperomia with small, patterned leaves resembling turtle shells, slower growing than other string plants.
commonExamples: Peperomia prostrata (String of turtles, Turtle vine), P. prostrata 'Variegata' (variegated form)
careTips: Water when top 2 inches of soil is dry. Keep slightly more moist than other string plants but still avoid overwatering. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Slower growing than other string plants. Perfect for hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Small patterned leaves resembling turtle shells. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Compact aloe with dark green to black-tinted leaves; same care as aloe vera. Toxic to pets.
commonExamples: Aloe 'Black Gem'
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 2-3 weeks). Bright indirect to direct light. Low humidity fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Hybrid echeveria with lavender-pink rosettes; powdery farina. Non-toxic to pets.
commonExamples: Echeveria 'Lola'
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Water at base to avoid farina. Bright light preferred. Low humidity fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Also known as: PVN. Popular echeveria with purple-pink rosettes and powdery farina; classic succulent. Non-toxic to pets.
commonExamples: Echeveria 'Perle von Nurnberg' (PVN)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Water at base to avoid farina. Bright light enhances color. Low humidity fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Also known as: Window plant. Haworthia with translucent "window" leaves; tolerates lower light than most succulents. Non-toxic to pets.
commonExamples: Haworthia cooperi (Window plant)
careTips: Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Bright indirect to medium light—tolerates lower light. Medium humidity fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Drought-adapted plants with water-storing leaves, need excellent drainage.
commonExamples: Echeveria, Sedum, Graptopetalum, Graptoveria
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 1-3 weeks depending on conditions). Water deeply but infrequently. Excellent drainage is essential - use cactus/succulent mix. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with succulent fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 2-3 years. Drought-adapted plants with water-storing leaves. Remove dead or dried leaves from the base. Prune leggy stems to promote compact growth. Allow cuts to callus before replanting.

description: Also known as: Golden barrel cactus. Round, barrel-shaped cacti that can grow quite large, very low-maintenance.
commonExamples: Echinocactus grusonii (Golden barrel cactus), Ferocactus (Barrel cactus), E. texensis (Horse crippler)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 3-4 weeks in summer, less in winter). Very drought tolerant. Full sun to bright indirect light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with cactus fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Can grow quite large. Repot every 3-5 years. Very low-maintenance. Handle with care - sharp spines. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Desert plants in the Cactaceae family with spines and areoles, need excellent drainage and bright light.
commonExamples: Echinocactus (Barrel cactus), Opuntia (Prickly pear, Bunny ears), Mammillaria (Pincushion cactus), Ferocactus
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 3-6 weeks). Water deeply but infrequently. Reduce significantly or stop watering in winter dormancy (November-February). Bright direct light essential - full sun preferred. Low humidity preferred. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with cactus fertilizer at quarter strength. Excellent drainage essential. Repot every 3-5 years. Handle with care - spines are sharp. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Also known as: True Christmas cactus. Forest cactus that blooms around Christmas, requires cool temperatures and reduced light to flower, has rounded leaf segments.
commonExamples: Schlumbergera × buckleyi (Christmas cactus, True Christmas cactus), S. truncata (Thanksgiving cactus, Crab cactus)
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist spring through summer. Reduce watering in fall (September-October) to encourage blooms - this triggers bud formation. More frequent watering than desert cacti. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct hot sun. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Cool temperatures (15-18°C) and reduced light in fall encourage flowering. Repot every 2-3 years. Rounded leaf segments distinguish from Thanksgiving cactus. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Forest cactus that blooms in spring, with rounded leaf segments.
commonExamples: Hatiora gaertneri (Easter cactus, syn. Rhipsalidopsis gaertneri)
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist spring through summer. Reduce watering in winter (December-February) to encourage spring blooms. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Cool temperatures in winter encourage flowering. Repot every 2-3 years. Rounded leaf segments. Blooms in spring (Easter time). Remove withered flowers and stem after flowering, except the 2-3 segments at the bottom of stem Remove spent flowers after blooming. Prune segments to shape after flowering.

description: Round or columnar cacti that produce large, funnel-shaped flowers in white, pink, or red, often opening at night.
commonExamples: Echinopsis spp. (Easter lily cactus)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; some morning sun is fine. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer. Large flowers bloom spring through summer. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Epiphytic woodland cactus with flat, leaf-like stems that produce spectacular nocturnal flowers in many colors.
commonExamples: Epiphyllum spp. (Orchid cactus)
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist spring through summer; reduce watering in winter. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid strong midday sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Epiphytic—use well-draining mix. Repot every 2-3 years. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Epiphytic cacti native to tropical forests, require different care from desert cacti with higher humidity needs.
commonExamples: Schlumbergera (Christmas cactus, Thanksgiving cactus), Rhipsalis (Mistletoe cactus), Epiphyllum (Orchid cactus, Queen of the night)
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist spring through summer. More frequent watering than desert cacti. Reduce watering in fall for bloom induction. Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun is fine. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Epiphytic cacti native to tropical forests. Repot every 2-3 years in well-draining mix. Different care from desert cacti. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Also known as: Moon cactus. Small, round cacti with chin-like notches above each areole; Moon cactus is a colorful grafted form.
commonExamples: Gymnocalycium mihanovichii (Moon cactus)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid intense direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer. Moon cactus is grafted—keep colorful top from burning. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Compact, round cacti with spiral tubercles and a crown of small flowers in spring.
commonExamples: Mammillaria spp. (Pincushion cactus)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect or direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer. Flowers form a ring around the crown in spring. Well-draining soil essential. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Round, woolly cactus covered in white hairs, produces pink flowers.
commonExamples: Mammillaria hahniana (Old lady cactus), M. bocasana (Powder puff cactus)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 3-4 weeks in summer, less in winter). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with cactus fertilizer. Well-draining soil essential. Covered in white hairs giving woolly appearance. Produces pink flowers in spring. Repot every 3-5 years. Compact, round growth habit. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Flat-padded cactus with glochids (tiny barbed spines) instead of large spines; handle with care.
commonExamples: Opuntia microdasys (Bunny ears, Polka dot cactus)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer. Handle with extreme care—glochids detach easily and are very irritating. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Round, ribbed cacti that produce yellow or golden flowers from the crown.
commonExamples: Parodia leninghausii, P. magnifica
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect or direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer. Golden flowers bloom spring through summer. Well-draining soil essential. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Flat-padded cacti in the Opuntia genus, can produce edible fruit, very low-maintenance.
commonExamples: Opuntia ficus-indica (Indian fig opuntia), O. microdasys (Bunny ears), O. humifusa (Eastern prickly pear)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 3-4 weeks in summer, less in winter). Very drought tolerant. Full sun to bright indirect light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize 2-3 times per year during growing season with cactus fertilizer. Well-draining soil essential. Flat, pad-like stems. Can produce edible fruit. Repot every 3-5 years. Handle with extreme care - tiny glochids are very irritating. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

description: Trailing cactus with long, thin stems covered in spines, produces bright pink or red flowers.
commonExamples: Aporocactus flagelliformis (Rat tail cactus), Disocactus flagelliformis
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 2-3 weeks in summer, less in winter). More water-tolerant than some cacti. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with cactus fertilizer at half strength. Trailing growth habit - perfect for hanging baskets. Produces bright pink or red flowers. Repot every 2-3 years. Long, thin trailing stems. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Epiphytic jungle cacti with branching, often pendulous stems; spineless and ideal for hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Rhipsalis baccifera (Mistletoe cactus), R. cereuscula (Coral cactus), R. pilocarpa (Hairy-stemmed rhipsalis), R. ewaldiana, R. mesembryanthemoides
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Epiphytic—well-draining mix. Trailing habit suits hanging baskets. Repot every 2-3 years. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Also known as: Giant cactus. Iconic columnar cactus of the Sonoran Desert, growing up to 12m tall with arm-like branches. Extremely slow-growing; takes 10 years to reach 2.5cm.
commonExamples: Carnegiea gigantea (Saguaro cactus)
careTips: Water deeply but infrequently — every 2-4 weeks in summer, monthly or less in winter. Requires full sun and excellent drainage. Use cactus mix with extra perlite. Extremely slow grower; indoor specimens rarely exceed 30cm. Tolerates extreme heat but protect from frost below -5°C. Fertilize once in spring with dilute cactus fertilizer. Non-toxic to pets. Remove any dead or damaged pads or segments with clean, sharp tools. Minimal pruning needed.

description: Small, round cactus with star-shaped pattern, very slow-growing and rare.
commonExamples: Astrophytum asterias (Star cactus, Sand dollar cactus, Sea urchin cactus)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry (every 3-4 weeks in summer, very little in winter). Very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Low humidity is fine. Fertilize sparingly (2-3 times per year) with cactus fertilizer at quarter strength. Well-draining soil essential. Very slow-growing. Star-shaped pattern on top. Produces yellow flowers. Repot every 3-5 years. Rare and protected in wild. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Crab cactus. Forest cactus that blooms in late fall, similar to Christmas cactus but with pointed leaf segments.
commonExamples: Schlumbergera truncata (Thanksgiving cactus, Crab cactus)
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist spring through summer. Reduce watering in fall (September-October) to encourage blooms. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Pointed leaf segments distinguish from Christmas cactus. Blooms in late fall (Thanksgiving time). Repot every 2-3 years. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

description: Compact flowering plants in the Gesneriaceae family with fuzzy leaves and colorful blooms, avoid getting water on leaves. Includes various cultivars with different flower colors, single, double, or ruffled flowers.
commonExamples: Saintpaulia ionantha (African violet), various cultivars with different flower colors, single, double, or ruffled flowers
careTips: Keep soil lightly moist. Always water from bottom or avoid wetting leaves - water on leaves causes permanent spots. Use room temperature water. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with African violet fertilizer to encourage continuous blooms. Repot annually in spring. Remove spent flowers. Crown rot is common - avoid overwatering. Remove dead and yellowish leaves and withered flowers

description: Classic tropical houseplant with glossy, heart-shaped spathes in red, pink, white, or coral that bloom year-round with proper care.
commonExamples: Anthurium andraeanum (Flamingo flower, Flamingo lily, Laceleaf), A. scherzerianum (Pigtail anthurium)
careTips: Water when top 2-3 cm of soil is dry; keep slightly moist but never soggy. Bright indirect light—direct sun bleaches spathes. High humidity (60%+) preferred; mist regularly or use a pebble tray. Well-draining, chunky aroid mix. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with quarter-strength phosphorus-rich fertilizer to promote flowering. Wipe leaves to remove dust. Toxic to pets (calcium oxalate crystals). Remove any rotting roots and damaged leaves promptly.

description: Cane begonias with wing-shaped spotted leaves and pendent flower clusters in red, pink, or white.
commonExamples: Begonia coccinea, B. 'Lucerna'
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; some morning sun is fine. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Prune leggy stems to encourage bushiness. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container.

description: Dramatic rhizomatous begonia with dark, textured leaves covered in cone-shaped black spikes (bullae). One of the most unusual-looking houseplants available. Native to limestone caves in Vietnam.
commonExamples: Begonia ferox (Fierce begonia)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry; avoid getting water on leaves. Bright indirect light — avoid direct sun. High humidity (60-70%) essential for best spike development. Extremely well-draining, chunite soil mix (perlite, bark, pumice). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with dilute balanced fertilizer. Grows naturally on limestone — benefits from slightly alkaline water or occasional crushed oyster shell in soil. Small white flowers appear in clusters. Cool to intermediate temperatures preferred — struggles above 27°C. Sensitive to root rot. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Cane begonia with silver-spotted leaves, red undersides, and white flower clusters. The most commonly sold form is the 'Wightii' cultivar.
commonExamples: Begonia maculata (Polka dot begonia, Spotted begonia), B. maculata 'Wightii' (most common cultivar)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Leaf spots fade in low light. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Rhizomatous begonia grown for its spectacular, multicolored foliage in swirling patterns of silver, purple, pink, red, and green. One of the most ornamental houseplant species.
commonExamples: Begonia rex-cultorum (Rex begonia, Painted-leaf begonia, King begonia), 'Escargot' (spiral pattern), 'Iron Cross', 'Fireworks', 'Silver Dollar'
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry completely. High humidity (60-70%) preferred — use pebble tray or humidifier. Bright indirect light maintains vibrant leaf colors; direct sun fades colors. Avoid wetting leaves which causes powdery mildew and spots. Water from bottom when possible. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 1-2 years. Ensure good air circulation. May go dormant in winter — reduce watering. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Silver vase plant. Bromeliads with pink flower spikes and silver-banded leaves.
commonExamples: Aechmea fasciata (Silver vase plant, Urn plant), A. 'Blue Rain'
careTips: Keep central cup (tank) filled with water at all times. Water soil when dry. Change cup water monthly to prevent stagnation and mosquito breeding. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall by adding diluted fertilizer to cup water. Flower spike lasts months. After flowering, plant produces offsets (pups) - parent plant dies but pups can be separated and repotted. In spring pruning and Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Colorful bromeliads with bright, long-lasting flower spikes.
commonExamples: Guzmania lingulata, G. 'Luna', G. 'Rana'
careTips: Keep central cup (tank) filled with water at all times. Water soil when dry. Change cup water monthly to prevent stagnation. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall by adding diluted fertilizer to cup water. Bright, long-lasting flower spikes. After flowering, plant produces offsets (pups) - parent dies but pups can be separated and repotted. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Tropical plants in the Bromeliaceae family with rosette growth and central cups (tanks) that hold water.
commonExamples: Guzmania (Flaming sword), Tillandsia (some species), Aechmea (Urn plant), Neoregelia (Blushing bromeliad)
careTips: Keep central cup (tank) filled with water at all times. Water soil when dry. Change cup water monthly to prevent stagnation and mosquito breeding. Bright indirect light preferred. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall by adding diluted fertilizer to cup water. After flowering, plant produces offsets (pups) - parent dies but pups can be separated. Most bloom once then produce pups. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage reblooming. Prune leggy growth after flowering season.

description: Shade-tolerant flowering plant with strap-like leaves and striking orange or yellow flower clusters.
commonExamples: Clivia miniata (Bush lily), C. nobilis
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Needs a cool, dry rest period (6-8 weeks in fall) with minimal watering to trigger blooming. Bright indirect light preferred; tolerates low light. Keep slightly pot-bound to encourage flowering. Fertilize monthly spring through summer. Toxic to pets. Remove dead and yellowish leaves and withered flowers

description: Glossy-leaved shrub that can produce white flowers and red coffee cherries indoors.
commonExamples: Coffea arabica (Arabian coffee)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Berries need several years to ripen. Acidic soil preferred. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage reblooming. Prune leggy growth after flowering season.

description: Thorny succulent shrub with colorful bracts that bloom year-round in bright light.
commonExamples: Euphorbia milii (Crown of thorns, Christ plant)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Milky sap is irritating—handle with care. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Tuberous flowering plants in the Primulaceae family with heart-shaped leaves and upswept flowers.
commonExamples: Cyclamen persicum (Florist's cyclamen), C. hederifolium (Hardy cyclamen), various colors
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. Water from bottom to avoid wetting leaves and crown. Cool temperatures (60-65°F) extend bloom time. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (50%) preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks during flowering with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Goes dormant after flowering - reduce watering and allow foliage to die back. Repot when dormant. Upswept, colorful flowers. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Cape jasmine. Fragrant flowering shrubs in the Rubiaceae family with glossy leaves and white blooms, require high humidity.
commonExamples: Gardenia jasminoides (Cape jasmine, Common gardenia), G. 'August Beauty', G. 'Veitchii'
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained (water when top inch is dry). Acidic soil essential (pH 5.0-6.5). Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun is fine. High humidity (60%+) essential - use humidifier. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks spring through fall with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Very fragrant white flowers. Prune after flowering. Can be finicky - requires consistent care. Repot every 2-3 years. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset.

description: Also known as: Transvaal Daisy, Barberton Daisy. Cheerful flowering perennial from South Africa with large, vibrant daisy-like blooms in many colors.
commonExamples: Gerbera jamesonii (Barberton daisy), G. 'Revolution' (compact series), G. 'Flori Line' (pot series), G. 'Garvinea' (garden series)
careTips: Bright indirect light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Water when top inch of soil dries — avoid wetting the crown to prevent rot. Well-draining, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5-6.5). Keep at 15-21°C for best flowering; avoid temperatures above 29°C. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continuous flowering. Non-toxic to pets.

description: Also known as: Florist's Gloxinia, Sinningia. Tuberous flowering plants in the Gesneriaceae family with velvety leaves and large, bell-shaped flowers.
commonExamples: Sinningia speciosa (Gloxinia, Florist's gloxinia), various colors and patterns
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. Water from bottom to avoid wetting leaves. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks during flowering with high-phosphorus fertilizer. Goes dormant after flowering - reduce watering and allow foliage to die back. Repot when dormant. Large, bell-shaped velvety flowers. Velvety leaves. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage reblooming. Prune leggy growth after flowering season.

description: Trailing gesneriad with waxy, tubular flowers resembling goldfish in orange, red, or yellow; ideal for hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Columnea gloriosa (Goldfish plant, Column flower), Nematanthus gregarius (Goldfish plant), Columnea microphylla
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Cooler, drier winter rest encourages spring blooming. Prune after flowering to maintain shape. Non-toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container.

description: Also known as: Chinese hibiscus. Showy shrub with large, colorful trumpet flowers that last one day but bloom repeatedly.
commonExamples: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis (Chinese hibiscus)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize weekly spring through fall with bloom fertilizer. Bud drop from stress or pests. Non-toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Wax plant. Classic wax plant with thick, waxy leaves and fragrant star-shaped flowers.
commonExamples: Hoya carnosa (Wax plant, Porcelain flower), H. carnosa 'Krimson Princess', H. carnosa 'Compacta'
careTips: Water when most of pot is dry (every 1-2 weeks). More drought tolerant than many houseplants. Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun encourages flowering. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Don't remove spent flower stems (peduncles) - they rebloom. Repot every 2-3 years. Fragrant star-shaped flowers. Can trail or climb. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Heart-shaped hoya often sold as single leaves, slow-growing but charming.
commonExamples: Hoya kerrii (Sweetheart hoya, Valentine hoya)
careTips: Water when most of pot is dry (every 1-2 weeks). Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Very slow-growing - single leaves may never grow into full plant. If you have a stem cutting (not just leaf), it will grow. Repot every 2-3 years. Charming heart-shaped leaves. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Epiphytic vines in the Apocynaceae family with waxy leaves and fragrant star-shaped flowers, also called wax plants.
commonExamples: Hoya carnosa (Wax plant, Porcelain flower), H. pubicalyx, H. kerrii (Sweetheart hoya, Valentine hoya)
careTips: Water when most of pot is dry (every 1-2 weeks). More drought tolerant than many houseplants. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Bright indirect light preferred; some direct morning sun encourages flowering. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Don't remove spent flower stems - they rebloom. Repot every 2-3 years. Fragrant star-shaped flowers. Can trail or climb. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Flame of the woods. Tropical shrub producing dense clusters of tiny star-shaped flowers in vibrant red, orange, yellow, or pink.
commonExamples: Ixora coccinea (Jungle geranium, Flame of the woods), I. chinensis, I. 'Nora Grant', I. 'Maui Yellow'
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist during growing season; reduce in winter. Bright direct to indirect light for best flowering. Medium humidity preferred. Acidic soil essential (pH 5.0-6.0)—iron chlorosis (yellow leaves) in alkaline soil. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with acid-forming fertilizer. Prune after flowering to maintain shape.

description: Also known as: Pink jasmine. Fragrant flowering vines in the Oleaceae family, popular for their sweet-smelling blooms.
commonExamples: Jasminum polyanthum (Pink jasmine), J. sambac (Arabian jasmine), J. officinale (Common jasmine)
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist (water when top inch is dry). Bright indirect to direct light preferred - more light encourages flowering. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through fall with high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage flowering. Provide support for climbing. Prune after flowering. Very fragrant flowers. Can be grown as houseplant or outdoor in warm climates. Repot every 1-2 years.

description: Also known as: Flaming Katy, Florist Kalanchoe. Colorful succulent houseplants with clusters of long-lasting blooms in red, pink, orange, yellow, and white. The most popular species is K. blossfeldiana.
commonExamples: Kalanchoe blossfeldiana (Flaming Katy), K. tomentosa (Panda plant), K. daigremontiana (Mother of thousands), K. pinnata (Cathedral bells)
careTips: Water when soil is completely dry — very drought tolerant. Bright indirect to direct light. Low humidity preferred. Well-draining succulent mix. Fertilize monthly during growing season. K. blossfeldiana needs short days (14+ hours darkness) for 6 weeks to rebloom. Deadhead spent flowers. Toxic to pets — contains cardiac glycosides.

description: Also known as: Lipstick vine. Trailing gesneriad with tubular red flowers emerging from dark calyxes like lipstick.
commonExamples: Aeschynanthus radicans (Lipstick vine)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; some morning sun encourages blooms. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Trailing habit suits hanging baskets. Non-toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.；remove peduncle after flowering

description: Vining plant with trumpet flowers in pink, red, or white; blooms from spring through fall.
commonExamples: Mandevilla sanderi (Rock trumpet)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect to direct light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize weekly spring through fall with bloom fertilizer. Provide trellis or support for climbing. Toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Rose Grape. Dramatic tropical houseplant with large, leathery leaves and cascading clusters of pink flowers that can last for months.
commonExamples: Medinilla magnifica (Rose grape, Philippine orchid, Showy medinilla)
careTips: Water when top 2-3 cm of soil is dry; reduce watering in winter. Bright indirect light—avoid direct sun which scorches leaves. High humidity (60%+) essential; mist daily or use a humidifier. Use well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix. Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through summer with half-strength balanced fertilizer. Needs a cool dry rest period (16-18°C) in winter to trigger reblooming. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
origin: Tropical forests in Philippines, Malaysia, and Indonesia

description: Aroids with white spathes and dark green foliage, excellent air purifiers, droop dramatically when thirsty as a watering indicator. Includes various cultivars ranging from compact to large.
commonExamples: Spathiphyllum wallisii (Peace lily), S. wallisii 'Domino', S. 'Sensation', S. floribundum, S. 'Mauna Loa'
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy, water when leaves droop slightly. Fertilize every 6-8 weeks during growing season. Remove spent flowers to encourage new blooms. Repot when roots fill container, typically every 1-2 years. Toxic to humans and pets if ingested; causes mouth irritation. Toxic to pets. Remove any rotting roots and damaged leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Moth orchid. Moth orchids, most common and beginner-friendly orchid genus in the Orchidaceae family with long-lasting blooms. Available in various colors.
commonExamples: Phalaenopsis (Moth orchid, Phal), various hybrid cultivars in many colors
careTips: Soak roots weekly for 15-20 minutes, then allow to dry between waterings. Never let sit in water. Avoid getting water in crown (center) which causes fatal crown rot. Use well-draining orchid bark mix, never regular potting soil. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. High humidity (50-70%) preferred. Fertilize weekly spring through fall with orchid fertilizer at quarter strength. Repot every 1-2 years when bark breaks down. Blooms last 2-3 months. Most beginner-friendly orchid. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage reblooming. Prune leggy growth after flowering season.

description: Also known as: Madagascar jasmine, Wax flower. Twining vine with waxy, tubular white flowers of exquisite fragrance, traditionally used in wedding bouquets.
commonExamples: Stephanotis floribunda (Madagascar jasmine, Bridal wreath, Wax flower)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist spring through fall; reduce in winter but don't let it dry out completely. Bright indirect light—some morning sun beneficial. High humidity (50-60%+) preferred. Well-draining potting mix. Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through summer with half-strength balanced fertilizer. Provide a trellis or hoop for climbing. Avoid moving once buds form—bud drop is common from changes in position or light. Cool winter rest (13-16°C) promotes flowering. Mildly toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Gesneriad with strappy leaves and trumpet flowers in blue, purple, pink, or white.
commonExamples: Streptocarpus spp. (Cape primrose)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Long blooming season. Non-toxic to pets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Flowering begonias grown from tubers, often with large showy blooms in various colors.
commonExamples: Begonia × tuberhybrida (Tuberous begonia), various hybrid cultivars
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist during active growth (spring through fall). Reduce watering significantly during dormancy period (winter) when leaves die back. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct hot sun. High humidity (50-60%) preferred. Fertilize every 2 weeks during active growth with high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage blooms. Store tubers dry in winter. Repot tubers in spring. Large showy blooms in various colors. Toxic to pets. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage reblooming. Prune leggy growth after flowering season.

description: Tropical plant with bold white-veined leaves and showy yellow bract flowers; requires consistent moisture and high humidity.
commonExamples: Aphelandra squarrosa (Zebra plant, Saffron spike zebra)
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. Bright indirect light essential. High humidity (60-70%) required—use pebble tray or humidifier. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Prone to leaf drop if care is inconsistent. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Compact prayer plant with light green leaves featuring bold dark green striping along the veins; folds leaves upward at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia concinna (syn. Calathea concinna 'Freddie')
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist but never soggy; use filtered or distilled water as sensitive to minerals and chlorine. Low to bright indirect light—no direct sun which scorches leaves. High humidity essential (60%+); use humidifier or pebble tray. Fertilize monthly spring through fall at quarter strength. Sensitive to drafts and temperature changes. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Peacock plant, Cathedral windows. Prayer plant with oval leaves featuring peacock-like patterns, leaves fold up at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia makoyana (Peacock plant, Cathedral windows), Calathea makoyana
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. High humidity (60%+) essential - use humidifier or pebble tray. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (prayer plant behavior). Repot every 1-2 years. Peacock-like pattern on leaves. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Popular prayer plant with dark green leaves and purple undersides, requires high humidity, leaves fold up at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia roseopicta 'Medallion' (Calathea medallion), G. roseopicta 'Dottie' (darker variety), G. roseopicta 'Rosy'
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (60-70%) essential - use humidifier or pebble tray. Use only distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning from minerals. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty). Repot every 1-2 years. Wipe leaves monthly. Sensitive to tap water and low humidity. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Stunning prayer plant with an intricate mosaic-like network pattern on its leaves that resembles stained glass or circuit boards, one of the most visually complex leaf patterns in nature.
commonExamples: Goeppertia kegeljanii (syn. Calathea musaica, Network calathea)
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged; very sensitive to drying out. Bright indirect light—no direct sun. High humidity (60%+) essential; leaf edges brown quickly in dry air. Use filtered or distilled water—sensitive to fluoride and chlorine in tap water. Well-draining, peat-based mix. Fertilize monthly spring through fall at quarter strength. Leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty). Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Round-leaved calathea. Large prayer plant with silver-striped round leaves, requires high humidity, leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty).
commonExamples: Goeppertia orbifolia (Calathea orbifolia, Round-leaved calathea)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (60-70%) essential - use humidifier. Use only distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun fades silver stripes. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty). Repot every 1-2 years. One of the larger calathea varieties. Wipe large leaves monthly. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Pin-stripe plant. Elegant prayer plant with dark green, glossy leaves adorned with thin pink or white pinstripes that fade to cream with age.
commonExamples: Goeppertia ornata (Pin-stripe calathea), G. ornata 'Sanderiana' (Broad-stripe calathea)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist; water when the top inch feels slightly dry. Medium indirect light is ideal — avoid direct sun, which scorches the delicate leaves. Maintain humidity above 60%; mist regularly or use a humidifier. Use filtered, distilled, or rainwater to prevent brown leaf edges from mineral sensitivity. Fertilize monthly during the growing season with a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer. Non-toxic to pets. Trim brown leaf edges with clean scissors. Remove yellowing leaves at the stem. Prune leggy stems to encourage fullness.

description: Prayer plant with wavy, patterned leaves resembling a rattlesnake's tail.
commonExamples: Goeppertia lancifolia (Calathea rattlesnake, syn. Calathea lancifolia)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (60-70%) essential - use humidifier. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Bright indirect light preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Wavy, patterned leaves resembling rattlesnake's tail. Repot every 1-2 years. Wipe leaves monthly. Sensitive to tap water and low humidity. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Rose painted calathea. Prayer plant with oval leaves featuring a bold pink or cream border on dark green, with purple undersides. Multiple popular cultivars.
commonExamples: Goeppertia roseopicta (Rose painted calathea), G. roseopicta 'Medallion', G. roseopicta 'Dottie' (nearly black leaves with pink outline), G. roseopicta 'Rosy' (pink center)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is slightly dry; keep consistently moist. Use filtered water. Medium indirect light preferred. High humidity (60%+) essential — brown leaf edges indicate low humidity. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Prayer plant with delicate white pinstripes on bright green, elliptical leaves. More compact than Calathea ornata with finer, more numerous stripes.
commonExamples: Goeppertia elliptica 'Vittata' (syn. Calathea vittata, White-striped calathea)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is slightly dry; keep consistently moist but not soggy. Use filtered water — sensitive to fluoride and chlorine. Medium indirect light; direct sun scorches leaves. High humidity (60%+) essential. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Prayer plant with variegated leaves in white, green, and lavender; leaves fold up at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia lietzei 'White Fusion' (syn. Calathea lietzei 'White Fusion')
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. High humidity (60%+) essential—variegation reverts in low humidity. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Prayer plant with bold white stripes on dark green leaves; leaves fold up at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia majestica 'Whitestar' (syn. Calathea 'White Star', Calathea majestica 'Whitestar')
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Prayer plant with velvety stripes alternating dark and light green; leaves fold up at night.
commonExamples: Goeppertia zebrina (syn. Calathea zebrina; Zebra plant)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Medium to high humidity (50-60%). Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold at night. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: Fishbone prayer plant. Prayer plants in the Marantaceae family with patterned leaves that fold up at night, more tolerant than some prayer plants.
commonExamples: Ctenanthe burle-marxii (Fishbone prayer plant), C. burle-marxii 'Amagris' (Golden Mosaic), C. setosa (Grey Star), C. oppenheimiana (Never-never plant), C. lubbersiana
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. High humidity (60%+) preferred - more tolerant than some prayer plants. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (prayer plant behavior). Patterned leaves. Repot every 1-2 years. Trim brown leaf edges with clean scissors. Remove yellowing leaves at the stem. Prune leggy stems to encourage fullness.

description: Also known as: Maranta Leuconeura. Classic prayer plant with red-veined leaves that fold up at night.
commonExamples: Maranta leuconeura (Prayer plant), M. leuconeura var. erythroneura (Red prayer plant), M. leuconeura var. kerchoveana (Rabbit tracks)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (60-70%) preferred - use humidifier or pebble tray. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Red-veined leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty). Repot every 1-2 years. Wipe leaves monthly. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Plants in Marantaceae family with leaves that fold up at night (nyctinasty), require high humidity.
commonExamples: Calathea (Goeppertia), Maranta leuconeura (Prayer plant), Stromanthe sanguinea
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist, never let dry. High humidity (60-70%) essential - use humidifier. Use only distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning from minerals. Bright indirect light preferred; direct sun burns leaves. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (nyctinasty). Repot every 1-2 years. Wipe leaves monthly. Sensitive to tap water, low humidity, and drafts. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Prayer plants in the Marantaceae family with colorful, patterned leaves that fold up at night.
commonExamples: Stromanthe sanguinea 'Triostar' (Tricolor stromanthe), S. sanguinea 'Magic Star' (spotted form), S. thalia
careTips: Keep soil consistently moist but not soggy. High humidity (60%+) essential - use humidifier or pebble tray. Bright indirect light preferred; avoid direct sun. Use distilled or filtered water to prevent leaf browning. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Leaves fold up at night (prayer plant behavior). Colorful, patterned leaves. Repot every 1-2 years. Remove yellowing or dead leaves promptly.

description: Tropical climbing vine with stunning elongated leaves featuring silver, green, and purple coloring with deep red-purple undersides, not a true begonia despite the common name.
commonExamples: Cissus discolor (Rex begonia vine, Tapestry vine)
careTips: Keep soil evenly moist but not soggy; sensitive to both drought and overwatering. Bright indirect light—direct sun fades the stunning leaf colors. High humidity (60%+) essential—drops leaves rapidly in dry air. Well-draining potting mix. Fertilize monthly spring through fall at half strength. Provide a trellis or moss pole. May go semi-dormant in winter, losing some leaves—reduce watering. Non-toxic to pets. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

description: Also known as: String of nickels. Epiphytic succulents related to Hoya, with coin-shaped or heart-shaped leaves; trailing or climbing habit.
commonExamples: Dischidia nummularia (String of nickels), D. ruscifolia
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Epiphytic—well-draining mix. Trailing habit suits hanging baskets. Repot every 1-2 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Classic trailing vine with lobed leaves, can be grown indoors or outdoors.
commonExamples: Hedera helix (English ivy, Common ivy), H. helix 'Glacier', H. helix 'Needlepoint'
careTips: Keep soil slightly moist. Cooler temperatures (60-70°F) preferred. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Prone to spider mites - mist regularly and inspect leaves. Prune to control length. Repot every 1-2 years. Can be grown indoors or outdoors. Toxic to pets.

description: Also known as: Venezuela Treebine. Trailing vine with glossy, grape-like trifoliate leaves. Excellent low-maintenance houseplant that tolerates lower light conditions and adapts well to indoor environments. Can trail from hanging baskets or climb a moss pole.
commonExamples: Cissus rhombifolia (Grape ivy, Oak leaf ivy), C. alata
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Allow to dry between waterings. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Prune to control length. Repot every 1-2 years. Easy-care houseplant. Grape-like leaves. Can trail or climb with support.

description: Vining Hoya with waxy, oval leaves and fragrant white flowers with red centers.
commonExamples: Hoya australis
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Allow soil to dry between waterings. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Compact, trailing hoya with small, pointed leaves and clusters of star-shaped, fragrant white flowers with pink or purple centers. One of the most popular hoyas for hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Hoya lanceolata subsp. bella (Hoya bella, Miniature wax plant, Beautiful hoya)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light encourages blooming. Do not remove spent flower stalks (peduncles) — new flowers emerge from the same spurs. Average to high humidity preferred. Fertilize monthly spring through summer. Mildly toxic. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Distinctive Hoya species with long, pointed leaves featuring prominent dark veining on a light green background, giving a stained-glass appearance. A highly sought-after collector Hoya.
commonExamples: Hoya callistophylla
careTips: Allow soil to dry between waterings. Bright indirect light for best leaf coloring; tolerates medium light. Do not remove flower peduncles as they rebloom from the same stalk. Well-draining aroid or orchid mix with bark and perlite. Fertilize monthly spring through fall. Slow to moderate grower. Leaves develop best venation pattern with good light. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Hoya carnosa cultivar with twisted, curled leaves creating a rope-like appearance; Hindu rope.
commonExamples: Hoya carnosa 'Compacta'
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Slow-growing. Waxy pink flowers when mature. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Compact Hoya species with small, thick oval leaves and fragrant yellow star-shaped flower clusters. One of the easier Hoyas to bring into bloom.
commonExamples: Hoya cumingiana
careTips: Allow soil to dry out between waterings — water thoroughly when dry. Bright indirect light encourages blooming; tolerates medium light. Do not remove spent flower stalks as new blooms emerge from the same peduncle. Well-draining mix essential — orchid bark, perlite, and peat. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Trailing Hoya with small, silver-mottled leaves; ideal for hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Hoya curtisii
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Compact growth. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Variegated wax plant. Popular variegated Hoya carnosa cultivar with creamy white to pink margins on waxy, semi-succulent leaves.
commonExamples: Hoya carnosa 'Krimson Queen' (Tricolor hoya, Variegated wax plant)
careTips: Allow soil to dry out between waterings; water thoroughly when the top 2-3 cm feel dry. Bright indirect light is essential to maintain variegation — some morning sun encourages pink tones on new growth. Use a well-draining, chunky mix with orchid bark and perlite. Maintain 40-60% humidity; tolerates average home humidity. Fertilize monthly in spring and summer with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Do not remove spent flower peduncles, as they rebloom from the same spurs. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Trailing Hoya with long, narrow, fuzzy leaves; pendulous habit suits hanging baskets.
commonExamples: Hoya linearis
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Fragrant white flowers. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Compact Hoya with silver-flecked leaves; hybrid of H. serpens × H. carnosa.
commonExamples: Hoya mathilde
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Slow-growing. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Large, round-leaved Hoya with thick, often silver-splashed foliage. Splash markings are the standard form. Produces fragrant star-shaped flower clusters.
commonExamples: Hoya obovata
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Pink flowers in clusters. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Fast-growing Hoya with silver-flecked leaves and fragrant dark pink or red flowers.
commonExamples: Hoya pubicalyx
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Bright indirect light preferred. Medium humidity (40-50%). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Prolific bloomer. Repot every 2-3 years when roots fill container. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Trailing hoya with narrow, elongated leaves edged in red or dark maroon, producing clusters of fragrant star-shaped flowers when mature.
commonExamples: Hoya wayetii, H. wayetii 'Variegata'
careTips: Allow soil to dry mostly between waterings (every 1-2 weeks). Bright indirect light preferred—some direct morning sun enhances leaf color. Medium humidity (40-50%) fine. Well-draining mix with perlite and orchid bark. Fertilize monthly spring through fall at half strength. Don't remove old flower stems (peduncles)—they rebloom. Let it become slightly rootbound for flowering. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

description: Also known as: Lemon-lime philodendron. Variegated heart-leaf philodendron with green and yellow-chartreuse leaves, easy-care trailing plant.
commonExamples: Philodendron hederaceum 'Brasil' (Brasil philodendron, Lemon-lime philodendron)
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Very forgiving of inconsistent care. Bright indirect light maintains variegation; tolerates low light but may lose variegation. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Fast-growing trailing plant. Prune to control length. Repot every 1-2 years. Green and yellow-chartreuse variegation. Toxic to pets.

description: Also known as: Silver pothos. Trailing aroids often called satin pothos, with silvery-splotched leaves, easy-care houseplants.
commonExamples: Scindapsus pictus (Satin pothos, Silver pothos), S. pictus 'Exotica' (large silver leaves), S. pictus 'Argyraeus', S. treubii 'Moonlight', S. treubii 'Dark Form'
careTips: Water when top inch of soil is dry. Very forgiving of inconsistent care. Bright indirect light maintains silvery variegation; tolerates low light. Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Trailing growth habit. Prune to control length. Repot every 1-2 years. Silvery-splotched leaves. Often called satin pothos but not a true pothos. Mildly toxic to pets -- causes mouth and skin irritation.

description: Trailing vine with heart-shaped, matte green leaves covered in silvery spots and patches. Not a true pothos despite the common name; belongs to the genus Scindapsus.
commonExamples: Scindapsus pictus 'Argyraeus' (Satin pothos), S. pictus 'Exotica' (larger silver patches), S. pictus 'Silver Ann' (mostly silver)
